amendments.rule: Reordered or discontinuous target tokens may occupy one unit when they realize one source item. Do not absorb unrelated intervening words into that unit. **Where English repeats one source function word because its scope is distributed across coordinated or emphatically repeated phrases or clauses, every English occurrence belongs to that source morpheme's one possibly discontinuous unit.** `מִן` in `מִבּוֹא בְדָמִים וְהוֹשֵׁעַ` → *from bloodguiltiness, and from avenging* takes both occurrences of *from*, while the waw takes only *and*; `בִּי אֲנִי` → *upon me ... upon me* gives both occurrences of *upon* to the single preposition while the suffix and explicit pronoun take their respective *me*. The repeated English word is neither `added` nor reassigned to a neighboring source item merely to make the units contiguous. **An explicit personal pronoun is read the same way where the ASV resumes it in a later clause of the same verse.** Where a following verbless clause writes no subject of its own and the ASV supplies the subject pronoun that an explicit `הוּא`, `הֵמָּה`, `אֲנִי` or the like standing earlier in the verse denotes, both occurrences belong to that pronoun's one discontinuous unit, exactly as rule 18 gives both pronouns of a twice-rendered suffix to the suffix and rule 20 gives both halves of an identifying formula to its one `הוּא`: `הֵמָּה סֹחֲרֵי יָדֵךְ ... בָּם סֹחֲרָיִךְ` → *they were the merchants of thy hand ... in these were* ***they*** *thy merchants* gives both *they*s to the one `הֵמָּה`, headed on the first. Such a pronoun is not `added`, and it does not join the predicate's unit: rule 20 hands the predicate the construction's copula and, in a presentative clause, its dummy *there*, and a referential pronoun is neither, so the clause's supplied *were* goes to the predicate while the pronoun goes to the morpheme that denotes it. This governs a clause with no subject of its own: where a finite verb stands in the resumed clause it takes the English subject pronoun under rule 17, which is a pronoun realizing that verb's own person and number. **And where the Hebrew stands the pronoun is not part of the condition.** Hebrew postposes an explicit subject pronoun after its predicate and that predicate's adjuncts, often before a coordinated second subject, while English writes a subject before its verb; where the ASV writes the pronoun in both places it has realized one written morpheme twice, and both occurrences are that pronoun's one discontinuous unit, headed on the first English occurrence: `וְהִנֵּה נִצָּב עַל־עֹלָתוֹ הוּא וְכָל־שָׂרֵי מוֹאָב` → *and lo* ***he*** *was standing by his burnt offering,* ***he*** *and all the princes of Moab* gives both *he*s to the one `הוּא`, while `נִצָּב` keeps the *was standing* rule 20 leaves it and the coordinated subject keeps its own English. So read whether one written pronoun is realized twice rather than which side of the resumption it stands on, and do not hand the first occurrence to the predicate to make the units contiguous: rule 17's permission reaches a pronoun realizing a finite verb's own person and number, and a participle or other predicate morpheme in a verbless clause takes only the copula. **And the morpheme that denotes the resumed subject need not be a pronoun.** Where a common noun or a proper name written in the verse is the referent the ASV resumes, every English realization of that referent belongs to the noun's one possibly discontinuous unit on exactly the terms above, headed on the first English occurrence: `עַל־אֱלוֹהַּ נוֹרָא הוֹד` → ***God*** *hath upon* ***him*** *terrible majesty* gives both *God* and *him* to the one `אֱלוֹהַּ`, and `שַׁדַּי לֹא־מְצָאנֻהוּ שַׂגִּיא־כֹּחַ` → *Touching* ***the Almighty****, we cannot find him out;* ***He*** *is excellent in power* gives the resuming *He* to `שַׁדַּי`, while `שַׂגִּיא` keeps the *is excellent* rule 20 leaves it. This is the preceding paragraphs' own reasoning read for the morpheme that is actually written — the pronoun goes to the morpheme that denotes it — since what licenses the English word is that the verse writes the referent, and not the part of speech the ASV first realized it by. Rule 17's ruling that a supplied lexical subject noun is `added` does not reach such a pronoun: that ruling governs an English noun answering to no morpheme at all, as `יָשְׁבוּ בָהּ` → *men shall dwell therein* is, and here a written nominal answers to it, so read whether the verse writes the referent before marking a supplied subject `added` or folding it into the predicate under rule 20. **But a morpheme already holding a pronoun of its own is not a home for a second one.** Where more than one morpheme in the verse denotes that referent, each takes only the English written for it, as rule 51 says of a waw and rule 43 of a spent preposition: the object suffix of `מְצָאנֻהוּ` above takes the *him* of *find him out* under rule 18, and the further *He* goes to `שַׁדַּי`. Count the ASV's realizations against the morphemes that could carry them, as rule 42 counts waws against *and*s. **An interrogative particle or a negative whose scope covers coordinated clauses is read the same way.** Where the Hebrew writes `הֲ` or `לֹא` once at the head of the first of two coordinated clauses and the ASV rewrites it at the head of the second, every occurrence belongs to that one morpheme's discontinuous unit, headed on the first: `הֲלוֹא מַחֲזֵה־שָׁוְא חֲזִיתֶם וּמִקְסַם כָּזָב אֲמַרְתֶּם` → ***Have*** *ye* ***not*** *seen a false vision, and* ***have*** *ye* ***not*** *spoken a lying divination* gives both *have*s to the `הֲ` and both *not*s to the `לֹא`, while each verb keeps only its own subject pronoun and lexical verb. This is rule 55's reading of a subordinator the ASV rewrites over a coordinated clause, applied to the particle that governs one. The second occurrence is neither `added` under rule 30 nor folded into the second clause's verb under rule 17. But read what is actually written before applying it: where the Hebrew gaps the morpheme in the second line and the ASV writes a single word carrying both the coordination and the negation, rule 35 governs and that word goes to the waw, as `לֹא עֲלִיתֶם ... וַתִּגְדְּרוּ` → *Ye have not gone up ..., neither built up* leaves the *neither* to the waw alone.
amendments.why: JOB.37 wrote the construction twice and the chapter analysed it two ways. Rule 25's resumption paragraph is framed on 'An explicit personal pronoun' and names `הוּא`, `הֵמָּה` and `אֲנִי`, so a pass meeting a written noun or proper name resumed by a supplied subject pronoun has three readings open to it and no sentence that closes them: rule 17 appears to make the pronoun `added`, rule 20 appears to let it ride along with the construction-supplied copula, and only rule 25's clause 'the pronoun goes to the morpheme that denotes it' — which is already lemma-neutral — points at the noun. JOB.37.22 took the noun and JOB.37.23 took the predicate. The amendment widens the paragraph to the morpheme that is written rather than its part of speech, which is what the surrounding sentences already reason from, and adds the count that keeps a suffix already holding its own pronoun from competing for the second one. Nothing in the precedent contradicts it: the corpus records no unit where a supplied referential subject pronoun is folded into a predicate's copula, and rule 20's own boundary already sends every supplied dummy but the presentative *there* out of the predicate's unit. Written as a qualification inside rule 25 rather than as a new rule, so the over-broad framing sentence is corrected where a later pass will read it.

conventions: Where a verse writes a nominal and the ASV resumes its referent as the supplied subject of a following clause that writes no subject of its own, both English realizations belong to that nominal's one discontinuous unit, headed on the first: אֱלוֹהַּ → *God ... him* (37.22) and שַׁדַּי → *the Almighty ... He* (37.23). The resuming pronoun is not added under rule 17 and does not join the predicate, which keeps only the construction-supplied copula. Where another morpheme in the clause already holds a pronoun of its own — the object suffix of מְצָאנֻהוּ, which takes the *him* of *find him out* — that morpheme is not a home for the second pronoun.

Heads on this chapter's multi-word substantive renderings were settled by rule 31's subtraction test, with its tie clause deciding two of them. עָב → *the thick cloud* heads on *cloud* and תֵּבֵל → *of the habitable world* heads on *world*, because the ASV writes a bare *cloud* for עָנָן in the same verse (37.11) and a bare *world* for תֵּבֵל as its ordinary rendering, making the modifier its specifier. נִפְלְאוֹת and מִפְלְאוֹת → *wondrous works* (37.14, 37.16), דָּרוֹם → *the south wind* (37.17) and זָהָב → *golden splendor* (37.22) head on the modifier, their English nouns being supplied generics the ASV never writes alone for those words.

report: Checked all 31 candidate lemma groups. Every multi-treatment bucket but one is the ASV rendering one morpheme differently in a context the source licenses: waw connectives (And, Likewise, Then, But, and the *which* of 37.5, where the waw's clause is recast as a relative with no explicit subject pronoun, rule 17); לֹא as a bare *not* beside the fused *cannot* of 37.5, 37.19 and 37.23 (rule 35, since יָכֹל is nowhere written); מִן as *out of*, *By* and *by reason of*; and the prepositions silenced at 37.2, 37.7, 37.16, 37.18 and 37.20, where the ASV promotes the governed noun to a direct or indirect object (rule 40), against those it renders in full.

אִם at 37.13 is not rule 14's correlative pair: the Hebrew writes three connectives for the ASV's *Whether ... or ... Or*, which is the אוֹ … אוֹ shape rule 14 excludes in its own terms, so each morpheme takes only the word written for it. The prepositional predicates were checked against each other as well: 37.10's בְּמוּצָק fuses to the single word *straitened* because the noun keeps no English of its own (rule 40's closing paragraph, rule 30), while 37.7's בְּיַד and 37.18's לִשְׁחָקִים leave their nouns a rendering and so go unrepresented. Both follow the same subtraction test.

Read the dump end to end for the 11 added units, which the lemma table cannot see. They divide consistently: a relative written over a finite clause the Hebrew wrote is added (37.2 *that*, over the written antecedent *sound*), while a relative that is part of a nominal's own recasting joins that noun (37.7 *whom he hath made* for מַעֲשֵׂהוּ, rule 46); supplied objects are added (37.7, 37.15, 37.19, rule 44); a connective or subordinator over a clause with no conjunction in it is added (37.19 *For*, 37.13 *that*) while every waw takes the word written for it; the impersonal *it* of the verbless 37.13 is added under rule 20, while the *it* of 37.20 realizes the Pual verb's own person and number under rule 17; and 37.22's *hath* is added because עַל already holds the written *upon* (rule 43's counting paragraph).

One real split, and it is invisible from inside either verse. At 37.22 the ASV realizes the single written noun אֱלוֹהַּ twice — *God ... him* — and both words go to that noun under rule 25. At 37.23 it resumes the written שַׁדַּי the same way — *the Almighty ... He* — but the verse pass folded that *He* into the predicate adjective שַׂגִּיא's unit. Rule 25 settles it: a referential pronoun is neither added nor the predicate's, and goes to the morpheme that denotes it. Patched 37.23; the copula *is* stays with שַׂגִּיא, and the object suffix of מְצָאנֻהוּ keeps the *him* already written for it, since a morpheme holding a pronoun of its own is not a home for a second one.

BSB: all eight disagreements are documented convention differences, not errors. Five are prepositions the ASV's recasting leaves nothing to say (rule 40), which BSB attaches to its phrase; אָרְצָה and its directive he at 37.12 are collapsed into the single rendering *the habitable world* (rule 22); the paragogic he of הַאֲזִינָה at 37.14 is rule 32's first sentence, which names this as the standard BSB divergence. No accepted edge was touched to improve the rate.

Heads on the chapter's multi-word substantive renderings differ by design and by rule 31's own tie clause, not by inconsistency: עָב → *the thick cloud* and תֵּבֵל → *the habitable world* head on the class noun because the ASV writes a bare *cloud* for עָנָן in the same verse and a bare *world* for תֵּבֵל ordinarily, while נִפְלְאוֹת → *wondrous works*, דָּרוֹם → *the south wind* and זָהָב → *golden splendor* head on the modifier, their nouns being supplied generics. Recorded as a convention so a later reader need not redo the test.
